course_information.title: Leadership & Managing a Retail Team
course_information.description: Build foundational skills in expectations, coaching, delegation, scheduling communication, and respectful team leadership.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; store-specific rules are not supplied
course_information.restrictions: No legal, tax, HR, accounting, or licensed-professional advice. Follow store procedures and refer restricted decisions.
learning_objectives: Give timely coaching based on behavior and outcomes.
Delegate work with authority, deadlines, and follow-up.
Respond fairly to team concerns and conflict.
Support safe, consistent customer service through daily leadership habits.

lessons.title: Set Clear Expectations
lessons.objective: Explain what successful work looks like.
lessons.why_this_matters: Employees cannot reliably meet expectations they have not heard or understood.

content_sections.heading: Make work observable
content_sections.text: Replace “keep the store nice” with specific tasks such as checking shelf labels, removing empty cartons, and clearing aisle hazards.

content_sections.heading: Define the standard
content_sections.text: Explain what needs doing, when it is due, and how to know it is complete. Ask employees to repeat the plan in their own words when helpful.

content_sections.heading: Keep standards consistent
content_sections.text: Use the same core expectations for similar roles. Adjust tasks for training, ability, accommodation, and authorized responsibilities as appropriate.

lessons.hardware_store_example: Before opening, a supervisor asks an associate to check the fastener aisle, remove empty packaging, and report missing shelf labels by 9:30.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Please check the fastener aisle before 9:30 and tell me which labels need replacing.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Giving vague instructions; assuming understanding; changing priorities without telling the team.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask the store manager or HR contact about accommodations, policy interpretation, or unclear job responsibilities.

lessons.title: Coach in the Moment
lessons.objective: Use specific, respectful feedback to improve performance.
lessons.why_this_matters: Small corrections made early are easier to act on than vague criticism later.

content_sections.heading: Describe what happened
content_sections.text: Focus on observable behavior rather than labels about a person. “The customer waited while you searched” is more useful than “You are careless.”

content_sections.heading: Explain the effect
content_sections.text: Connect the behavior to safety, customer experience, or team workflow. Invite the employee to describe what happened.

content_sections.heading: Agree on a next step
content_sections.text: Demonstrate the expected action, invite practice, and follow up. Recognize improvement when you see it.

lessons.hardware_store_example: An employee leaves a customer without explaining they are checking inventory. A supervisor privately models a short update and practices it with the employee.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “When you need to check stock, tell the customer what you are doing and when you’ll return.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Correcting someone publicly when privacy is possible; making assumptions about intent; offering no next step.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Use established HR procedures for repeated misconduct, discrimination concerns, or serious safety violations.

lessons.title: Delegate with Follow-Through
lessons.why_this_matters: Delegation creates capacity only when employees have the information and authority to succeed.

content_sections.heading: Match task and readiness
content_sections.text: Consider training, workload, and safety authorization. Do not delegate regulated or hazardous work to an unqualified employee.

content_sections.heading: Clarify the handoff
content_sections.text: State the outcome, deadline, resources, decision limits, and check-in time. Give employees room to complete the task within those boundaries.

content_sections.heading: Close the loop
content_sections.text: Review completion, remove obstacles, and recognize progress. Avoid repeatedly taking the task back unless safety or urgency requires it.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A manager delegates an endcap refresh to a trained associate, shares the approved planogram, sets a noon check-in, and identifies who can approve substitutions.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Use this approved layout. Let me know by noon if an item is unavailable.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Delegating without a deadline; assigning work without authority; micromanaging every step.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate staffing constraints, restricted equipment use, and decisions outside the employee’s role.

lessons.title: Handle Concerns and Conflict Respectfully
lessons.objective: Respond fairly to team disagreements and concerns.
lessons.why_this_matters: Unresolved conflict can affect service, safety, and trust.

content_sections.heading: Listen separately when needed
content_sections.text: Hear each person’s account without assuming who is right. Ask about specific actions and dates, not rumors.

content_sections.heading: Use the right channel
content_sections.text: Handle routine task disagreements with coaching. Follow HR and reporting policies for harassment, discrimination, threats, retaliation, or other serious concerns.

content_sections.heading: Agree on practical next steps
content_sections.text: Clarify expectations, document as required by policy, and check whether the problem is resolved. Protect confidentiality to the extent appropriate.

lessons.hardware_store_example: Two associates disagree over who should restock a display. The supervisor reviews assignments and workload, listens to both, and clarifies the next shift’s responsibilities.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “I want to understand what happened and clarify the work so this does not repeat.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Taking sides before hearing facts; discussing private concerns with unrelated coworkers; ignoring serious reports.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Immediately involve the designated manager or HR contact for threats, harassment, discrimination, or safety risks.

lessons.title: Lead a Consistent Daily Huddle
lessons.objective: Use short team check-ins to align priorities.
lessons.why_this_matters: A few minutes of clear communication can prevent repeated questions and missed tasks.

content_sections.heading: Start with priorities
content_sections.text: Share the day’s key customer-service goals, deliveries, promotions, and safety reminders. Keep the message short.

content_sections.heading: Invite useful questions
content_sections.text: Ask what could block progress and who needs support. Confirm which employee owns each priority.

content_sections.heading: Review and adjust
content_sections.text: At the end of the shift, note what was completed and what needs handoff. Do not share confidential employee or customer information in a group huddle.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A morning huddle covers an incoming truck, a weekend paint promotion, and a blocked receiving aisle. The team assigns owners and a check-in time.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Our priorities are a clear receiving aisle, accurate sale signs, and helping customers quickly. What might get in the way?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Listing too many priorities; using huddles to embarrass staff; skipping follow-up.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unsafe conditions, staffing shortages, or unresolved customer issues to the responsible leader.

options.A: Discuss private personnel issues in detail
